title: Naming a child
hookLine: a hukam is taken and the child named with the first letter of the hymn

lines: A BABY IN A CAR SEAT.
THE GRANTH OPENED WHERE IT FALLS.
cards: A new baby asleep in a car seat on the carpet of a gurdwara. Grandparents on one side, a nervous father on the other, the mother holding a bowl of karah prashad. Hymns of thanks are sung.
Then the person attending the Granth opens it, not at a marked page but wherever it falls, and reads the hymn at the top of the left-hand page. Everyone leans in for one thing: the first letter.
Somebody whispers a name they've been hoping for, and it fits. Somebody else is already counting names on their fingers. That letter is where this child's name begins.

teach.b: Naam karan means the naming. The Sikh Rehat Maryada describes it, in paraphrase: when mother and child are able, the family comes to the gurdwara with karah prashad. Hymns of joy and thanks are sung.
A hukam is taken, the way we met last week: the Granth opened at random and the hymn at the top of the left-hand page read.

teach.h: A HUKAM GIVES THE FIRST LETTER.
teach.b: The first letter of that hymn is announced, and a name beginning with it is chosen. Then the code adds a second name: Singh for a boy, Kaur for a girl. Ardas is said, and the prashad shared.
Two things to hold. First, who chooses.

teach.h: A NAME CHOSEN FROM THE LETTER.
teach.b: The Granth gives a letter, not a name. People still choose, so the name is both gift and choice: the Guru's word and human love meeting on one letter. Second, the second name.

teach.h: SINGH OR KAUR FOR EVERY CHILD.
teach.b: The code gives a boy Singh and a girl Kaur, whatever family they're born into. Some readers see a quiet answer to caste in that: a surname can carry a caste, and Singh and Kaur carry none.
Earlier this week the code said no caste; here, some would say, it's written into the name.
And the week, looking back: end well, pray while cooking, explained, no lucky days, a tenth, crowned, and now the name from the hukam, where a life's name begins in the Word.

how: Sikh families bring a new baby to the gurdwara with karah prashad; a hukam is taken from the Guru Granth Sahib, its first letter is announced, a name beginning with it is chosen, and Singh or Kaur is added.

o: the ceremony when a child first ties a turban
a vow to repeat God's Name each morning and evening
the Sikh naming, its first letter taken from a hukam

games.q: inside the naming: tap the pairs.
p: the second name the code adds

s: the Granth gives the child's whole name
it gives a first letter. a name beginning with it is chosen.
Singh is added for a boy and Kaur for a girl
the code adds them, whatever family the child is born into.
the naming happens on a day chosen by the stars
the family comes when mother and child are able. the code rejects lucky days.

games.q: the hukam is read and the letter announced. what happens next?
o: the first word of the hymn becomes the name.
a name beginning with that letter is chosen.
the Granth is opened again until a favorite letter comes up.
games.why: the Granth gives the letter; people choose the name. the Guru's word and human love meet on one letter.

practice: Say your own name once, slowly, in your head, and think about who chose it and what they might have hoped.
If you know its meaning, hold that for a few breaths; if not, hold the hope instead, then let the name rest the way a hymn rests after it's read.

wordCard.voice: Naam karan. The Sikh naming: a hukam is taken, the first letter of the hymn is announced, a name is chosen from it, and Singh or Kaur is added. Today's word.
